question: A 25-year-old haemodynamically stable man sustains an isolated closed femoral shaft fracture. After resuscitation with 1 L crystalloid and 2 units PRBC, his BP is 110/70 mmHg and HR is 88/min. What is the MOST appropriate definitive management?

answers.text: Skin traction for 6 weeks followed by functional bracing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Skin traction is obsolete as definitive treatment for adult femoral shaft fractures. Prolonged bed rest causes thromboembolic complications, fat embolism, and delayed mobilisation.

answers.text: Closed intramedullary interlocking nail (IMIN) — early within 24–48 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. IMN is the gold standard for closed femoral shaft fractures in adults. Early fixation (within 24–48 h in haemodynamically stable patients) reduces blood loss from fracture haematoma, lowers fat embolism risk, enables early mobilisation, and reduces ICU stay.
Incorrect. DHS is used for intertrochanteric fractures, not diaphyseal shaft fractures. IMN is appropriate for shaft fractures.

Incorrect. External fixation is used as a temporary measure (damage-control orthopaedics) in haemodynamically unstable or polytrauma patients. It is not the definitive treatment for isolated femoral shaft fractures.

overallFeedback.feedback: Key fact: IMIN is the definitive treatment for adult femoral shaft fractures. Early nailing in stable patients reduces FES risk, VTE risk, and allows faster mobilisation. External fixation is only a bridge (damage-control) in unstable polytrauma.

Correct. Closed intramedullary interlocking nailing is the gold standard for adult femoral shaft fractures. Advantages: load-sharing construct, early weight-bearing, low complication rate, shorter hospital stay. Early fixation (within 24–48 h) is preferred in stable patients.
